title: Aurora Borealis
full_review:
Cantankerous elderly Ronald, whose Parkinson's disease is realistically etched by Donald Sutherland, claims he can see the northern lights from his Minneapolis window.

The thusly named "Aurora Borealis" (Regent) tells the story of Duncan (Joshua Jackson), Ronald's unmotivated 25-year-old grandson, who takes a maintenance job at an assisted living facility for the elderly to be near him and his caring wife, Ruth (Louise Fletcher).

Duncan's commendable altruism stands in sharp contrast to his philandering, well-heeled brother, Jacob (Steven Pasquale) who, wife and kids notwithstanding, uses Duncan's apartment for extramarital trysts, which Duncan passively allows.

Both Duncan and his grandfather are tortured by mostly unspoken memories of Duncan's father, who died (possibly of drug use) years earlier. This mutual grief provides a unique bond.

On the romantic front, Duncan has been a loner until he falls in love with his granddad's home health aide, Kate (Juliette Lewis), a plain-spoken gal who pushes him to shake out of his lethargy and focus on continuing his education and living up to his potential.

James Burke's downbeat, albeit well-intentioned, film scores points for its compassionate portrayal of the elderly, and advocacy of familial responsibility in caring for them, but the script is dramatically sluggish, and the nonstop barrage of bad language -- however true to the milieu -- regrettable. There are several poignant moments, as when Ronald needs to go to the bathroom while he and Duncan are at a shopping mall, and Duncan must help him navigate, much to their mutual embarrassment. Apart from a passionate but clothed groping between Duncan and Kate, there are no sex scenes.

There is one troubling story aspect from a Catholic standpoint: Brent Boyd's script goes beyond empathizing with Ronald's fervent wish to be spared a debilitating decline into almost making a case for euthanasia, as the old man repeatedly asks Duncan to assist him in ending his life. However, without spoiling anything, the matter is skirted by a plot twist, and there is a morally sound (if improbable) resolution.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language, a euthanasia theme, adultery, acceptance of premarital sex, some heavy groping and innuendo, a couple of violent brawls and a drug reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
